To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the molecular nature of shark calcified extracellullar matrix, and its relationship with tetrapod skeletal tissues, remains poorly understood, and we here provide the first comparative analysis of the molecular footprint of shark and frog skeletal tissues.
the molecular nature of shark and tetrapod endoskeletal elements is distinct and that the vertebral cartilages of both species share a conserved molecular footprint, which suggests a common origin.

we identified the expression of Col2a2 in vertebral cartilage, which is the first evidence of Col2a in a cartilaginous tissue, and we identified the expression patterns of Col1a, Col2a and Col10a in shark and frog skeletal tissues, which allowed us to compare the molecular footprint between the two vertebrate lineages and discuss the evolutionary history of the vertebrate calcification process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary origin of the vertebrate calcified matrix, and the diversification of skeletal tissues during vertebrate evolution.
the molecular nature of skeletal cell types and tissues, and the evolutionary changes associated with the diversification of the calcified vertebrate skeleton.
the molecular footprint of the vertebrate endoskeleton, and its evolution, and represents a step forward in our understanding of the evolution and diversification of vertebrate calcified tissues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vertebrate skeletal calcification is a mosaic of molecular footprints that can be traced back to the last common ancestor of all vertebrates.
the shark vertebral cartilage is a calcified cartilage, but not a true endochondral bone.

the shark skeleton has a complex molecular organization that is not easily comparable to the one found in osteichthyans, and that the tetrapod endoskeleton is not the result of a single step of skeletal evolution, but of several steps, some of which may have occurred in the shark lineage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the molecular footprinting of the vertebrate calcified extracellular matrices, and their associated cells, is a powerful approach to understand the molecular basis of skeletal evolution in vertebrates.

the molecular footprint of the shark skeleton is more complex and diverse than previously thought, and that this complexity is not restricted to the cartilaginous endoskeleton, but is also observed in the endochondral skeleton of tetrapods.
, despite the presence of conserved features in the molecular footprint of skeletal tissues, we have identified several derived features that have been acquired in the tetrapods.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the molecular footprint of vertebrate calcified tissues, including cartilage, is more diverse than anticipated and is subject to evolutionary changes, which may be linked to changes in the developmental context of skeletal calcification.
the molecular nature of vertebrate skeletal tissues has been shaped by a combination of conserved and derived mechanisms.

, despite their different skeletal architectures, the molecular footprints of the endoskeletons of Scyliorhnius and Xenopus are surprisingly similar, and that the molecular signatures of the endochondral ossified tissues of both species are strikingly similar.
